accuracy.evidence: Advice matches the PSHE Association Key Stage 2 programme of study (set goals, break them into achievable steps, recognise progress) and the executive-function literature on planning and task initiation (Harvard Center on the Developing Child: planning and self-regulation develop through middle childhood). The frog-poster order (facts, plan, draw and write, check) follows the plan-draft-revise-edit writing process taught in KS2 English. Every arithmetic item (steps left, days, minutes per step) was checked at the corners of its parameter ranges.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented slips: waiting to feel ready before starting (first prediction and the 'wait' challenge option), steps that restate the whole job ('Finish the whole story tonight', 'Learn all 10 spellings tonight'), vague steps that cannot be ticked off ('Get better at spelling', 'Do some spelling stuff'), cramming on the last night, doing steps out of order, and counting only what is left instead of what is done.

lab_distinct.evidence: The mechanics are this topic's own: a boulder that shrinks as each step is chipped off it, an order board where only the correct next step is accepted with a reason, a small-and-clear vs too-big-or-fuzzy sorter, a re-split of steps that are still too big, and stepping stones that require a progress check before the next stone. It differs from flagtry (persistence), flaghabit (habit loops) and flagwproc (writing-process vocabulary) and passed the 30% shingle gate.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child experiences the job getting smaller before being told why, discovers that steps have a necessary order through the refusal reasons, learns the test of a good step (you know what to do and when it is done), learns that a step can be split again, and practises acknowledging progress after each step: the three evidence statements of the topic (list three or more steps, start with the first step, acknowledge progress).

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions with tempting wrong options: 'Wait until you feel like it' for a too-big job, 'Learn all 10 tonight' as a first spelling step, and 'Skip it for today' when 'Write the story' still feels too big. Each is disproved by the step's own feedback.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating scenarios (Lego set, book report, step 1 of 5, perfect room, times-table test) with ten distinct m= messages naming the slip: everything at once, waiting to feel ready, cramming, wrong order, counting only what is left, finished steps not counting, trying harder at a giant step, giving up, and fuzzy steps.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences and everyday jobs (room, poster, spellings) and read well under the family kid limit; the adult text was simplified from FK 10.8 to 7.8 after the first validator run. Canvas text is one short heading per step with wrapped step cards.

no_filler.evidence: Passed the filler regex and the 12% duplicate gate. Kid text covers why big jobs stall, chunking, the small-and-clear test and starting plus noticing progress; adult text covers curriculum placement, first-step size and order, named mistakes, and what the lab does.

mobile.evidence: Checked 360 px screenshots of all six steps at start and after Show me in light and dark: the chipped steps sit in a 2x2 grid with wrapped text, the four order slots and four loose cards fit, both sort bins fit side by side, the three split options are full width, and the four stones fit with labels; the white tick on light-green stones in dark mode was changed to dark text after the screenshots.

accessibility.evidence: walk.cjs: axe WCAG 2.1 AA clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13, every task completes with Show me, the challenge shows, no console errors. Every canvas action has a button (break off a step, Step n: card buttons, Too big / Small and clear, split option buttons, stone and self-talk buttons) and the canvas aria-label reports each result.
